tier_reason: The first-party report compares Corosio against Boost.Asio coroutines and callbacks, and the benchmark code is public in bench/corosio, bench/asio/coroutine and bench/asio/callback. The test environment says only 'Windows (IOCP backend)', with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so the entry cannot be tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 9-50% faster handler dispatch than Asio coroutines (e.g. concurrent post/run: 2.35 Mops/s vs 1.61 Mops/s, +46%); best multithreaded scaling (retains 89% of single-thread throughput at 8 threads vs 58% for Asio coroutines and 53% for Asio callbacks; 1.54 vs 1.03 / 1.51 Mops/s at 8 threads). Losses: Asio callbacks are 51% faster on single-threaded post (2.59 vs 1.71 Mops/s), Asio is 2.5-2.6x faster on 64KB bidirectional throughput (5.74 GB/s vs 2.18 GB/s), and Asio is ~10x faster on timer schedule/cancel (historical; that timer API has since been removed). Socket latency and HTTP server results are ties (within 5%).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 84 stars; developed under the C++ Alliance (cppalliance) GitHub organization
corrections.caveats: Unusually candid report that documents losses as well as wins. Benchmark code is public (bench/), but the report states no CPU model, compiler or flags, so it is capped at tier C. Windows/IOCP only in this report. The default branch is develop; there is no main branch.

notes: The recorded benchmark_url pointed at a main branch that does not exist (404), so it now points at develop; master holds an older copy with near-identical numbers. The record's claim that Asio's own maintainers maintain the project could not be verified (Asio lives at chriskohlhoff/asio), so it was removed from stars_or_usage. All other metadata checked out: BSL-1.0, not archived, not a fork, 84 stars, last commit 2026-09-25.

tier_reason: WS_BENCHMARK.md compares the project against tungstenite 0.30 and tokio-tungstenite 0.30 using public bench code (benches/, `cargo bench --bench ws`). The numbers come from a shared Windows machine with no CPU model or rustc version, so this is first-party evidence with partial methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Codec vs tungstenite: 2.3-2.6x faster masked encode at 64B, ~10x faster masked encode at 256KiB, parity at 16KiB. Echo loop 64B: 26.5 us/msg vs 37.2 us/msg for tokio-tungstenite (page: 1.4-1.5x faster at 64B/1KiB; ~29% lower latency, derived from page data). The echo result is a tie with sync tungstenite (26.5 vs 26.5 us). Losses: 9% behind tungstenite at 16KiB echo, 2-3x behind at 256KiB with both ends courierust, and 1.9x slower UTF-8 validation than std::str::from_utf8.
corrections.workload: WebSocket codec encode/decode (no sockets) and loopback-TCP echo round trips plus one-way push, at 64B-256KiB payloads; single cargo bench --release run in one process on a shared machine (the suite also runs in CI)
corrections.caveats: Licensed under PolyForm Perimeter 1.0.1 (LICENSE file; GitHub reports NOASSERTION), a source-available, non-OSI license. No CPU model or rustc version is given. The echo win is only against async tokio-tungstenite; sync tungstenite ties at 64B/1KiB and wins at 16KiB and 256KiB. The authors note that large-payload numbers varied 3-10x across repeated runs on shared hardware.

notes: All claimed numbers appear in WS_BENCHMARK.md, but the record left out the ties and losses against sync tungstenite; claimed_speedup and caveats now include them. The page's numbers are not CI output: CI (Github_Action_Benchmark.md) runs on an unspecified Linux runner and gives no CPU model. Metadata checked: 5 stars, last commit 2026-09-15, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: The README 'Benchmark Results' table compares exec-rs directly against a Tokio echo server (examples tokio_echo vs exec_echo) and supports the claimed 10-26% (104,601/114,478/107,333/85,745 vs 114,723/130,694/135,157/100,321 req/s). No hardware, compiler, load generator or run methodology is given, so this is first-party evidence without methodology.

corrections.workload: Single-threaded TCP echo server (exec_echo example on the P2300-style sender/receiver design vs the tokio_echo example): Light (50 connections), Medium (200), Heavy (500) and Large (4KB payload; connection count not stated)
corrections.caveats: The README and Cargo.toml declare Apache-2.0, but the repository has no LICENSE file and GitHub detects no license, so treat it as reference only. No hardware, compiler or load-generator details are given for the benchmark. Single-threaded mode only.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. baseline_in_list is now false: Tokio is not in the event-loops incumbent list (libuv/libevent/epoll/io_uring) and not in known_list.txt.
